result.summary: Demeter, disguised as an old woman named Doso, tells the daughters of Celeus a false story of being kidnapped by pirates. They take her to their mother Metaneira, who offers her the nursing of her late-born son. Demeter sits in grief until Iambe's jests make her smile, and she refuses red wine.

scenes.title: Demeter's false tale at the well
scenes.summary: The maidens ask the old woman who she is. Demeter invents a story of pirates and escape and asks for work in a household.
scenes.stakes: Demeter, searching for her daughter in disguise, needs shelter and must hide her identity.

scenes.title: Callidice offers a home
scenes.summary: Callidice names the city's leaders and proposes that Metaneira take the stranger in as nurse. The girls run home and bring Demeter back.
scenes.stakes: Demeter needs a welcome in a mortal household.

scenes.title: Demeter in the house of Celeus
scenes.summary: Demeter fills the doorway with radiance, and Metaneira is awed. Demeter sits veiled and silent until Iambe's jests make her smile, then she refuses red wine and takes a drink of meal, water and mint.
scenes.stakes: Demeter's grief over her lost daughter, and the risk of her divinity being seen.

scenes.title: Metaneira's offer
scenes.summary: Metaneira welcomes the stranger and asks her to nurse her son, promising great reward.
scenes.stakes: Metaneira hopes to secure care for her long-awaited son.

alias_notes.explanation: False name Demeter gives herself while disguised.

notable_quotes.reason: Expresses the human acceptance of what the gods send, a recurring theme.

analysis.text: A god in disguise tests mortal hospitality; her grief and divine radiance show through the mask.
The refusal of red wine for a mixed drink of meal, water and mint echoes the kykeon of the Eleusinian Mysteries.

legacy.text: Iambe's jesting is often linked to the ritual obscene joking at Demeter's festivals and to the origin of iambic verse.

fun_facts.text: A lacuna after line 211 means some verses of the hymn are lost in the manuscript.

language_notes.text: "Old mother" is a respectful form of address to an elderly woman; "of folk born long ago" means she seems to belong to an earlier generation.
"Hail" is a greeting, here meaning "greetings" or "good health to you."
Doso means "giver" in Greek, a fitting false name for the goddess who gives grain and gifts.
Thoricus is a place on the coast of Attica, near Athens, so the invented story brings her close to where she actually is.
"Unpurchased" means without payment: the pirates would have sold her as a slave overseas, so she escaped before they could profit.
"Recess of the well-built chamber" means an inner nook of the bedroom where the master's bed stood.
"Perforce" means by necessity; mortals have no choice but to endure what the gods send.
"Coif of towers" is a metaphor for the city's crown of towers, i.e. its battlements, which the leaders guard.
"Late-born" means born after the parents' other children, when they were no longer young; hence he is much prayed for.
"Any one of womankind who should see you would envy you" means any woman would envy you the rich rewards you would receive.
"Hire" means wages; "measureless" means unlimited, a very generous payment.
"Hinds" are female deer; "sated" means fully fed.
The veiled head and dark cloak signal Demeter's mourning for her lost daughter.
"Scion" means a young offspring or descendant; here it is the infant son Demophoon, described as a tender shoot.
"Jointed seat" is a folding or joined stool, a simple seat of fitted pieces, contrasted with the bright couch.
"Pleased her moods in aftertime also" means Iambe's jesting continued to soothe the goddess in later times, hinting at a ritual origin of ribald jokes.
"Not lawful" means forbidden for her in her grief; red wine was refused, and the mint drink (kykeon) became the Eleusinian ritual drink.
"Deo" is another name for Demeter. The text breaks off here at a gap in the manuscript.
"Perforce" means of necessity; mortals must endure what the gods send whether they like it or not.

context_notes.text: Pirate raids and enslavement of captives were a real danger in the ancient Mediterranean, so the story would seem believable to the maidens.
Callidice is one of the daughters of Celeus, the ruler of Eleusis, whose household will take Demeter in.
Triptolemus, Dioclus, Polyxeinus, Eumolpus and Dolichus are Eleusinian nobles. Triptolemus and Eumolpus are later linked with Demeter's mysteries at Eleusis.
Metaneira is the wife of Celeus, ruler of Eleusis, the "brave father" of the girls.
The infant is Demophoon, whom Demeter will later try to make immortal.
Demeter is the goddess of grain and harvest, hence "bringer of seasons." She is disguised as an old woman searching for her daughter Persephone.
Iambe's joking is traditionally linked to the bawdy jesting at Demeter's festivals; the word "iambic" in poetry is also associated with her name.
Metaneira's son was born late in her life; in the wider story the child is Demophoon, whom Demeter tries to make immortal.

literary_notes.text: "That queen among goddesses" reminds us of Demeter's true rank while she appears as a humble old woman.
The audience knows Demeter is a goddess and her story is invented, while the maidens take it as true.
Her gracious blessing and modest request present her as a polite, harmless suppliant, helping win the girls' trust.
Callidice calls the stranger "godlike" without knowing she truly is a goddess.
The girls are compared to bounding deer and calves, conveying their youthful energy and joy; the crocus simile for their hair adds color.
The goddess's slow, grieving walk behind the girls follows their joyful dash, emphasizing her sorrow.
The goddess's head touching the roof and the doorway filled with light signal her divinity breaking through her mortal disguise.
Listing awe, reverence and pale fear builds Metaneira's overwhelming reaction and shows the goddess's power.
Demeter's long silence, refusal of food and never smiling vividly portray her grief for Persephone.
The yoke on mortals' necks pictures human subjection to divine will as a burden borne like an ox's.
Metaneira offers a stranger her child, unaware she is a goddess; the reader knows Demeter will treat him in extraordinary ways.
